page_intro: I work at the intersection of diplomatic, intellectual, and cultural history, with a focus on the institutions and people who mediated the Cold War divide.

items.title: Cultural Diplomacy & Academic Exchange
items.summary: Fulbright, public diplomacy, academic mobility, information policy, and the institutions that connected the United States with East-Central Europe.
items.body:
My work on cultural diplomacy examines how Cold War programs designed to influence societies across the Iron Curtain produced consequences that often exceeded — and sometimes contradicted — the intentions of policymakers. Academic exchange became part of the struggle for influence, but it also created relationships, habits of cooperation, and intellectual networks that could not be fully controlled from Washington, Warsaw, or Moscow.

Poland is at the center of this research, viewed within the broader history of East-Central Europe and its changing relationship with Russia. I am particularly interested in what survived the Cold War itself: how exchanges and personal connections formed before 1989 helped shape the region’s post-communist orientation, its relationship with the United States, and the  emergence of a transatlantic political and intellectual community after the collapse of the Soviet bloc.
items.related: Fulbright · public diplomacy · Voice of America · academic mobility · Polish-American relations.

items.title: The Great Alternative: Rethinking East-Central Europe
items.summary: Networks linking Polish émigré political thought with American foreign policy, and changing visions of Eastern Europe during the Cold War and beyond
items.body:
At the center of this research is what I call the “Great Alternative”: the attempt to imagine an East-Central Europe no longer organized around Russian domination or the political order created at Yalta. I trace how this alternative took shape in the dialogue between the Paris-based émigré journal Kultura, one of the most influential centers of postwar Polish political thought, American Sovietology, and policy circles, and how ideas initially developed at the margins of Cold War politics gradually entered broader debates about the future of the region.

Jerzy Giedroyc, the editor of Kultura and a major architect of postwar Polish thinking about East-Central Europe, and Zbigniew Brzezinski, the Polish-born American strategist and Sovietologist who later served as U.S. National Security Advisor, stand at the center of this history. I am currently preparing an edition of their correspondence, but my interest extends beyond their personal relationship to the political world that connected them: competing understandings of Russia and Ukraine, the nationalities question in the Soviet Union, détente, and the possibility of a post-imperial order in Eastern Europe. I am especially interested in how ideas that once appeared politically improbable became part of the intellectual vocabulary through which the transformations of 1989–1991 — and their unfinished consequences — were understood.
items.related: Kultura · Sovietology · détente · Brzezinski · Giedroyc · intellectual networks.

items.title: Ukraine, Sovereignty & Émigré Thought
items.summary: Ukrainian émigré intellectual history, Soviet federalism, state-making, and the emergence of Ukrainian and East-Central European studies in North America.
items.body:
The Ukrainian question within the Soviet empire stands at the center of this part of my research. I examine the tension between Soviet federalism and imperial rule: how institutions created to contain and manage national difference could, over time, provide languages of sovereignty, political legitimacy, and statehood that Moscow had never intended to empower.

I am equally interested in the relationship between Ukrainian émigré thought and developments inside Soviet Ukraine. Rather than treating exile and the homeland as separate worlds, I trace how political ideas, interpretations of the Soviet system, and expectations about Ukraine’s future developed through their interaction. Émigré scholars also played an important role in challenging views of Ukraine as simply part of a Russian-dominated Soviet space and in placing it within a broader East-Central European frame.

This interest in the Ukrainian question also informs my work on the unexpected consequences of Soviet federalism. In studying what I call “republican uncivil society,” I ask how institutions and political networks created to govern Soviet republics acquired interests and capacities of their own — and how, as the Union center weakened, structures designed to administer Soviet Ukraine could become instruments of republican sovereignty and, eventually, statehood.

From there, my research extends to Ukraine’s place in what I describe as the “Soviet West” and to the longer history of Russian-Ukrainian relations. I am interested in how Soviet and imperial arrangements shaped competing understandings of Ukraine’s relationship with Russia and Europe, and how some of these tensions survived the collapse of the Soviet Union and continue to shape the region today.
items.related: Soviet federalism · sovereignty and statehood · Russian-Ukrainian relations · émigré thought · Ukrainian studies
